summary: This memo proposes a standard for message encapsulation, meaning forwarding one or more messages inside another. It also defines "bursting," which unpacks forwarded messages so they can be distributed, forwarded, or replied to.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 934 proposes a way to put one or more mail messages inside a new message and later extract them. It defines boundary lines and a way to protect lines inside a forwarded message that might otherwise look like boundaries.

questions: how to forward messages by encapsulation
what is message bursting in email
what is message encapsulation in email
how does mail digest bursting work
what is character stuffing in rfc 934
subtitle: A proposed format for wrapping mail messages so a recipient can extract them again.

tldr.problem: Forwarded messages and digests need clear boundaries so recipients can separate and process the original messages.
tldr.mechanism: A forwarding agent places messages between dash-led boundaries and adds a dash and space before any message line that could be mistaken for a boundary.
tldr.outcome: The memo proposes an encapsulation and bursting format for discussion, and argues that ordinary users should forward messages rather than redistribute them as if original.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 934's status as Unknown, and no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo is a proposed protocol and explicitly requests discussion and suggestions for improvement.

sections.title: Forwarding and Bursting Messages
sections.content:
The memo focuses on forwarding, where a user agent places one or more received messages in the body of a new message. A digest can be treated as a forwarded collection. The recipient needs a way to separate the enclosed messages so they can be read, replied to, or handled individually.

RFC 934 calls the extraction process bursting. It proposes a common format because existing digest formats were ambiguous, blind-carbon-copy behavior differed among user agents, and the authors wanted forwarding and distribution to use a related procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: Forwarding several messages in one body makes them hard to handle separately unless the boundaries are clear. Bursting is the process of extracting those messages again.

sections.title: The Message Boundaries
sections.content:
The proposal uses a forwarding agent to compose the outer message and a bursting agent to split it later. The outer message has a header and a text portion, separated by a blank line. Within the text, a line beginning with a dash is an encapsulation boundary.

The text can contain an initial part, the enclosed messages, and a final part. Each enclosed message has a header and a body; its header must include at least a Date field and a From field. Addresses in those headers must be fully qualified.
sections.plainLanguage: The outer message can include introductory text, enclosed messages, and a closing text. Dash-led lines mark the boundaries, and each enclosed message needs Date and From headers.

sections.title: Protecting Boundary-Like Lines
sections.content:
A forwarded message may itself contain a line beginning with a dash. To prevent a bursting agent from treating that line as an outer boundary, the forwarding agent adds a dash and a space before it. During bursting, a boundary beginning with dash-space is treated as message text, and the extra prefix is removed.

This character-stuffing rule supports recursive forwarding. The memo also discusses blank lines around boundaries for compatibility with existing agents, while saying a strictly conforming forwarding agent should not generate those blank lines.
sections.plainLanguage: If an enclosed message has a line that looks like a boundary, the sender marks it with an extra dash and space. The recipient recognizes the mark and restores the original line.

sections.title: Blind Copies and Distribution
sections.content:
The memo discusses ways to send blind carbon copies. Its suggested method sends a normal visible message and a separate blind message that contains the visible message as an enclosed forward. This avoids giving blind recipients a copy that lists the visible recipients in a way that could lead to an accidental reply to everyone.

The document distinguishes forwarding from distribution, where a received message is reposted as a processable original. It encourages distribution by trusted discussion-group agents but argues that individual users should forward a message inside a new draft instead.
sections.plainLanguage: For a blind copy, the memo suggests sending the blind recipient a separate message containing the visible message as an enclosed forward. This helps prevent an accidental reply that includes the visible recipients.
